title: Adaptive throughput validation protocol and acceptance harness
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Create a reproducible, customer-facing validation protocol and load harness for Dedicated capacity throughput guarantees. The goal is to provide artifacts and a runnable harness that: (1) emulates realistic sequence-length distributions and KV-cache warmup, (2) exercises autoscaler hysteresis and burst policies, (3) injects tenant contention and noisy neighbors, and (4) produces a standardized benchmark report and acceptance checklist that sales/SEs can share with customers for SLA signoff.
acceptance_criteria: Harness can reproduce three canonical profiles: conversational low-latency, long-sequence batch, and mixed multi-tenant traffic
End-to-end benchmark run produces a signed report with 50th/90th/95th/99th latency and per-token cost estimates
Autoscaler behaviour validated: scale-up latency < configured SLO and scale-down does not cause request failures during tapering window
KV-cache warmup strategy included and measurable: cache-warm run vs cold-run delta documented
Customer acceptance checklist completed and validated with one pilot customer (internal staging tenant)
Runbook for interpreting results, re-running under identical seeds, and capturing artifacts (logs, flamegraphs, traces) is present
load_harness_design: Lightweight controller written in Go + Python drivers. Components: 1) Traffic generator supporting per-profile sequence length distribution, prompt templates, and streaming vs non-streaming modes; 2) Tenant mixer to simulate multi-tenant contention with configurable QPS ratios; 3) KV-cache warmers that prepopulate caches using representative prefixes; 4) Autoscaler perturbation module to inject synthetic load spikes and step-down windows; 5) Result aggregator that pulls Datadog/Prometheus metrics and collects trace/log bundles. Harness exposes deterministic seeds and a manifest describing the workload configuration.
benchmarking_methodology: Benchmarks run in three phases: A) Warmup (15-30 minutes) to stabilize caches and JITs; B) Baseline sustained run (90 minutes) at target throughput levels to measure steady-state latency and resource utilization; C) Perturbation tests with controlled spike and recovery windows to evaluate tail-latency and autoscaler responsiveness. Use percentile-aware sampling, keep input random seeds recorded, and run each scenario 3 times to calculate mean and standard deviation. Normalize cost to per-1M tokens using measured GPU utilization and token counts. Include a reproducibility score indicating what fraction of runs were within a 5% envelope for 95th percentile latency.
test_plan: 1) Define canonical profiles and target throughput (e.g., 500 req/s for conversational, 80 req/s for long-sequence batch, and mixed 3:1:1 tenant split). 2) Run warmup until KV-cache hit-rate stabilizes (>90% for cached profile). 3) Execute baseline run and capture latencies, GPUs utilization, memory, queue depths, and errors. 4) Execute perturbation scenarios: burst 2x/3x for 60s, sudden drop for 2 minutes, network noise simulation (packet loss 0.5%-1%). 5) Run autoscaler hysteresis sweep: vary scaleUpThreshold and scaleDownDelay to observe oscillation regimes. 6) Produce final report and attach artifacts to ticket.
customer_acceptance_steps: Share harness manifest and reproducibility instructions with customer contact
Run pilot in customer staging with identical harness config and capture their logs
Walk customer through report: steady-state throughput, tail-latency, cost-per-token, and scaling behavior
Obtain signoff via acceptance checklist and add to account SOW for Dedicated contract
runbook: Step 0: Pull latest harness binary and verify git commit hash. Step 1: Provision ephemeral Dedicated cluster with tracing enabled and a single model variant. Step 2: Upload prompt templates and set manifest seeds. Step 3: Start warmup, monitor kv_cache_hit_rate, and wait until stable. Step 4: Kick off baseline run and record metrics. Step 5: Run perturbations and autoscaler sweep. Step 6: Collect traces (Jaeger), flamegraphs, and Datadog dashboards. Step 7: Run analysis script to generate PDF report and upload artifacts to shared drive. Step 8: If metrics fail acceptance criteria, revert autoscaler config to last-known-good and open ENG follow-up.
risks: False confidence from synthetic-only workloads: mitigate by ensuring customer-profile mirroring. Autoscaler tests may induce transient request errors in production-like environments — always run on staging or ephemeral accounts. Cost of long runs on large clusters is non-trivial; include budget estimates in PRDs. Race conditions in KV-cache warmers can produce inconsistent hit rates; include randomized start-order to detect fragility.
